eng1-w1-q1.question: Which word has a silent 'k'?
eng1-w1-q1.explanation: In 'knee' the k is silent; the word is pronounced like 'nee'. In kite, kick and bake the k is clearly pronounced.

eng1-w1-q2.question: In which word is the letter 'h' silent?
eng1-w1-q2.explanation: In 'honour' the h is silent; the word begins with the vowel sound 'o', which is why we say 'an honour'. In hotel the h is pronounced in today's standard English, and that is the common trap.

eng1-w1-q3.question: How is the '-ed' in 'wanted' pronounced?
eng1-w1-q3.explanation: The last sound of 'want' is t, and after t or d the -ed forms an extra syllable 'id': wan-tid. The 't' sound appears in words like walked, where the sound before it is voiceless.

eng1-w1-q4.question: In which word is the final '-s' pronounced like 'z'?
eng1-w1-q4.explanation: The last sound of 'dog', g, is voiced, so the -s sounds like 'z': 'dogz'. In cats, books and maps the sounds before it (t, k, p) are voiceless, so there the -s stays an 's' sound.

eng1-w1-q5.question: Which pair of words differs ONLY in voicing (one first sound is voiced, the other voiceless, made in the same way)?
eng1-w1-q5.explanation: f and v are both made with the upper teeth and the lower lip; the only difference is that v has vibration in the throat. In fan/pan both f and p are voiceless, in sip/ship both s and sh are voiceless, and in bat/mat both b and m are voiced.

eng1-w1-q6.question: Which word does NOT begin with a vowel sound?
eng1-w1-q6.explanation: 'university' begins with the letter u, but its sound is 'yoo', which is a consonant sound, so we say 'a university'. In hour and honest the h is silent (vowel sound), and umbrella begins with the vowel sound 'uh'. Trap: don't answer by looking at the letter; listen to the sound.

eng1-w1-q7.question: In which word is the letter 'b' silent?
eng1-w1-q7.explanation: In 'thumb' the b after m is silent; the word sounds like 'thum' (as in comb and climb). In table, rubber and bright the b is clearly pronounced.

eng1-w1-q8.question: Which of these consonant sounds is voiceless (no vibration in the throat)?
eng1-w1-q8.explanation: There is no vibration in the throat when you say 's', so it is voiceless. v, z and d are voiced sounds; their voiceless partners are f, s and t. Put your hand on your throat and say 'sss' and 'zzz' to check.

eng1-w1-q9.question: How is the final '-es' in 'dishes' pronounced?
eng1-w1-q9.explanation: The last sound of 'dish' is 'sh', and after s, z, sh or ch the -es forms an extra syllable 'iz': 'dish-iz'. Saying just 's' or 'z' would sound like 'dishs', which is wrong.

eng1-w1-q10.question: In which word is the '-ed' pronounced as 'd'?
eng1-w1-q10.explanation: The last sound of 'clean' is the voiced 'n', so the -ed sounds like 'd': 'cleend'. cooked (k), kissed (s) and laughed have a voiceless sound before the -ed, so it is pronounced 't'. Trap: 'laughed' is written with 'gh', but the sound is 'f', which is voiceless.

eng1-w1-q11.question: How many sounds (not letters) are there in the word 'thick'?
eng1-w1-q11.explanation: 'thick' has 5 letters but only 3 sounds: 'th' + 'i' + 'k'. 'th' is two letters making one sound, and 'ck' is also a single 'k' sound. 4 comes from counting one of these pairs as two sounds, and 5 is the number of letters.

eng1-w1-q12.question: In which group is the final '-s' pronounced 'z' in ALL three words?
eng1-w1-q12.explanation: bags (g), pens (n) and trees (the vowel 'ee') all have a voiced sound before the -s, so all three take 'z'. cups (p) and books (k) have a voiceless sound before it, so they take 's'. In roses, the last sound of 'rose' is 'z', so the -s forms an extra syllable 'iz', not just 'z'.

eng1-w1-q13.question: In which group does the '-ed' add an extra syllable in EVERY word?
eng1-w1-q13.explanation: need, add and wait all end in a t or d sound, so in all three the -ed adds an extra syllable 'id': nee-did, a-did, way-tid. played takes just a 'd' sound, and fixed (ks) and laughed (f) take just a 't', with no new syllable. Trap: saying 'fix-id' because of the spelling.

eng1-w1-q14.question: Which word has a silent letter AND a final '-s' pronounced 'z'?
eng1-w1-q14.explanation: In 'knees' the k is silent, and the sound before the -s is the voiced vowel 'ee', so the -s is pronounced 'z': 'neez'. 'knocks' also has a silent k, but the 'k' sound before its -s is voiceless, so it takes 's'. 'dogs' has 'z' but no silent letter, and 'maps' has neither.

eng1-w1-q15.question: In how many of these words is the '-ed' pronounced as 't': stopped, begged, hated, missed, laughed?
eng1-w1-q15.explanation: stopped (p), missed (s) and laughed (the 'f' sound) have a voiceless sound before the -ed, so all three take 't': a total of 3. begged has the voiced g, so it takes 'd', and hated adds the extra syllable 'id' after t. Traps: leaving out laughed because of its 'gh' spelling (2), or counting hated too (4).

eng1-w2-q1.question: How many syllables are there in the word 'computer'?
eng1-w2-q1.explanation: com-pu-ter: three vowel sounds, so 3 syllables. Don't count letters or vowels; count only the separate vowel sounds you hear when you say it.

eng1-w2-q2.question: In 'The principal will present the prizes', where is the stress on 'present'?
eng1-w2-q2.explanation: Here 'present' is an action (verb) meaning 'to give', so the stress is on the 2nd syllable: pre-SENT. It is PRES-ent when it is a noun (gift) or an adjective.

eng1-w2-q3.question: Which word is stressed on the SECOND syllable?
eng1-w2-q3.explanation: be-GIN is a 2-syllable verb stressed on the 2nd syllable. DOC-tor, HAP-py and WIN-dow are all stressed on the 1st syllable.

eng1-w2-q4.question: The word 'photography' has four syllables: pho-tog-ra-phy. Which syllable is stressed?
eng1-w2-q4.explanation: In words ending in -graphy the stress falls on the third syllable from the end, so pho-TOG-ra-phy (2nd syllable). Trap: 'PHO-to-graph' is stressed on the 1st syllable, so students apply the same pattern here too.

eng1-w2-q5.question: The word 'education' has four syllables: ed-u-ca-tion. Which syllable is stressed?
eng1-w2-q5.explanation: The stress falls on the syllable just before -tion, so ed-u-CA-tion (3rd syllable). -tion itself is never stressed; it is said lightly as 'shun'.

eng1-w2-q6.question: In which sentence is the word in quotes stressed on the FIRST syllable?
eng1-w2-q6.explanation: In 'a lovely present', present is a noun (gift), so PRES-ent. The other three (object, record, permit) are verbs here, so their stress is on the 2nd syllable: ob-JECT, re-CORD, per-MIT.

eng1-w2-q7.question: How many syllables are there in the word 'elephant'?
eng1-w2-q7.explanation: el-e-phant: three vowel sounds, so 3 syllables. 'ph' is a single 'f' sound. Eight is the number of letters, not syllables; don't count vowel letters, listen to the sounds as you say the word.

eng1-w2-q8.question: Which word is stressed on the FIRST syllable?
eng1-w2-q8.explanation: 'toothbrush' is a compound noun (tooth + brush), and compound nouns are usually stressed on the first part: TOOTH-brush. de-CIDE, re-LAX and be-GIN are two-syllable verbs stressed on the 2nd syllable.

eng1-w2-q9.question: In 'about' (a-BOUT), how is the unstressed first 'a' pronounced?
eng1-w2-q9.explanation: The first 'a' is in an unstressed syllable, so it becomes a weak 'uh' (schwa): uh-BOUT. Saying a full 'a' as in 'cat' or 'ay' as in 'day' is wrong, because this syllable is weak. And the a is not silent, because it forms a syllable of its own.

eng1-w2-q10.question: The word 'electricity' has five syllables: e-lec-tric-i-ty. Which syllable is stressed?
eng1-w2-q10.explanation: The stress falls on the syllable just before -ity, so e-lec-TRIC-i-ty (3rd syllable). Trap: 'e-LEC-tric' is stressed on the 2nd syllable, but adding -ity moves the stress forward. The 'i' is part of -ity itself, so it is not stressed.

eng1-w2-q11.question: 'Ravi is a rebel; he will rebel against any unfair rule.' How are the two words 'rebel' stressed?
options: The 1st one on its 2nd syllable, the 2nd one on its 1st syllable
The 1st one on its 1st syllable, the 2nd one on its 2nd syllable
eng1-w2-q11.explanation: The first 'rebel' ('a rebel') is a person, a noun, so it is stressed on the 1st syllable: REB-el. The second, 'will rebel', is an action (a verb), so it is stressed on the 2nd syllable: re-BEL. In noun-verb pairs the noun is stressed first and the verb later; giving both the same stress is the common mistake.

eng1-w2-q12.question: In which sentence is the word in quotes stressed on the SECOND syllable?
options: The police caught the 'suspect' near the station.
The soldiers did not 'desert' their posts.
Camels can survive for days in the 'desert'.
The 'conflict' between the two clubs lasted a year.
eng1-w2-q12.explanation: In 'did not desert their posts', desert is a verb (to abandon), so de-SERT. The other three are nouns: SUS-pect (the person the police catch), DES-ert (sandy land) and CON-flict (a fight), so they are stressed on the 1st syllable. Trap: 'desert' appears in two options with the same spelling; check the part of speech first.

eng1-w2-q13.question: Where is the stress in 'photographic' (pho-to-graph-ic)?
eng1-w2-q13.explanation: The stress falls on the syllable just before -ic, so pho-to-GRAPH-ic (3rd syllable). Traps: copying the pattern of PHO-to-graph (1st) or pho-TOG-ra-phy (2nd). When the suffix changes, the stress moves too: PHO-to-graph, pho-TOG-ra-phy, pho-to-GRAPH-ic.

eng1-w2-q14.question: Which word is stressed on the THIRD syllable?
eng1-w2-q14.explanation: in-for-MA-tion: the syllable just before -tion is 'ma', the 3rd. bi-OL-o-gy (-logy), pho-TOG-ra-phy (-graphy) and a-BIL-i-ty (-ity) are all stressed on the 2nd syllable. Apply each word's suffix rule, then count the syllables.

eng1-w2-q15.question: Which word has exactly THREE syllables?
eng1-w2-q15.explanation: de-ci-ded: 'decide' has 2 syllables, and after d the -ed adds an extra syllable 'id', making 3. In watched the -ed is just a 't' sound (1 syllable), wanted has 2 (wan-tid), and educated has 4 (ed-u-ca-ted). Trap: treating every -ed as an extra syllable.

eng1-w3-q1.question: In 'She sings beautifully', the word 'beautifully' is:
eng1-w3-q1.explanation: 'beautifully' tells us how she sings, i.e. it modifies the verb 'sings', so it is an adverb. 'beautiful' (without -ly) would be an adjective, as in 'a beautiful song'.

eng1-w3-q2.question: Which word is a pronoun in 'Ravi gave them a book'?
eng1-w3-q2.explanation: 'them' is used in place of the names of some people, so it is a pronoun. Ravi and book are nouns, and gave is a verb.

eng1-w3-q3.question: In 'He works hard', the word 'hard' is:
eng1-w3-q3.explanation: Here 'hard' tells us how he works, i.e. it modifies the verb 'works', so it is an adverb. Trap: in 'a hard question', hard is an adjective, because there it describes a noun.

eng1-w3-q4.question: In 'We waited until the rain stopped', the word 'until' is:
eng1-w3-q4.explanation: 'until' is followed by a full clause ('the rain stopped', which has both a subject and a verb), so here it is a conjunction. In a phrase like 'until Monday' (just a noun) it would be a preposition.

eng1-w3-q5.question: Which word is an adjective in 'The tired children fell asleep early'?
eng1-w3-q5.explanation: 'tired' describes the noun 'children', so it is an adjective. 'early' here tells us when they fell asleep, i.e. it modifies the verb, so it is an adverb.

eng1-w3-q6.question: In which sentence is 'round' used as a preposition?
options: They will round the figure off to 50.
The earth goes round the sun.
eng1-w3-q6.explanation: In 'round the sun', round shows a relation (direction) with the noun 'sun', so it is a preposition. In 'a round face' it is an adjective, in 'the first round' a noun, and in 'round the figure off' a verb.

eng1-w3-q7.question: Which word is a verb in 'Priya bought a new laptop'?
eng1-w3-q7.explanation: 'bought' (the past form of buy) shows an action, so it is a verb. Priya and laptop are nouns, and 'new' describes the laptop, so it is an adjective.

eng1-w3-q8.question: Which word is an interjection in 'Ouch! I hit my toe on the door.'?
eng1-w3-q8.explanation: 'Ouch!' shows a sudden feeling of pain, so it is an interjection. 'hit' is a verb, and toe and door are nouns.

eng1-w3-q9.question: In 'The cat is sleeping under the table', the word 'under' is:
eng1-w3-q9.explanation: 'under' shows the cat's position in relation to the noun 'the table', so it is a preposition. A conjunction would be followed by a full clause (subject + verb), which is not the case here.

eng1-w3-q10.question: In 'She is a friendly teacher', the word 'friendly' is:
eng1-w3-q10.explanation: 'friendly' describes the noun 'teacher', so it is an adjective. Trap: calling it an adverb because of the -ly. friendly, lovely and lonely are adjectives even though they end in -ly.

eng1-w3-q11.question: Which word is a noun in 'Her honesty impressed everyone'?
eng1-w3-q11.explanation: 'honesty' is the name of an idea (a quality), so it is a noun, even though you cannot touch it. 'Her' shows possession, 'impressed' is a verb, and 'everyone' is a pronoun. Trap: thinking only people and things are nouns; names of ideas are nouns too.

eng1-w3-q12.question: In which sentence is 'fast' used as a verb?
options: He runs fast in every race.
It is a fast train to Delhi.
She held fast to the rope.
eng1-w3-q12.explanation: In 'Many people fast', fast is an action (going without food) and it comes in the verb position after the subject 'people', so it is a verb. In 'runs fast' it is an adverb (how he runs), in 'a fast train' an adjective (it describes the train), and in 'held fast' also an adverb, because the verb there is 'held'.

eng1-w3-q13.question: In which sentence is 'after' a conjunction?
options: She left after we had finished dinner.
eng1-w3-q13.explanation: In 'after we had finished dinner', after is followed by a full clause (subject 'we' + verb 'had finished'), so it is a conjunction. In 'after the class' and 'after the bus' only a noun follows it, so it is a preposition. In 'soon after' nothing follows it and it only tells us when, so it is an adverb.

eng1-w3-q14.question: How many adverbs are there in 'She spoke very softly yesterday'?
eng1-w3-q14.explanation: softly (how she spoke), yesterday (when she spoke) and very (it modifies softly: how much) are all adverbs, so 3. Traps: counting only the -ly word 'softly' (1), or leaving out one of 'very' and 'yesterday' (2). 'She' is a pronoun and 'spoke' is a verb.

eng1-w3-q15.question: In which sentence is 'that' used as a pronoun?
options: That car belongs to my uncle.
I know that he is honest.
eng1-w3-q15.explanation: In 'That is my new phone', that stands alone as the subject in place of a thing (a noun), so it is a pronoun. In 'That car' and 'that tall building', that comes before a noun and points to it, so it works like an adjective (determiner). In 'I know that he is honest', that joins two clauses, so it is a conjunction.

eng1-w4-q1.question: Water ___ at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
eng1-w4-q1.explanation: This is a scientific fact that is always true, so simple present 'boils'. 'is boiling' would be used if some specific water were boiling right now.

eng1-w4-q2.question: Look! The baby ___.
eng1-w4-q2.explanation: 'Look!' shows that the action is happening right at this moment, so present continuous 'is sleeping'. 'sleeps' is for habits, not for an action happening now.

eng1-w4-q3.question: I ___ him at the library yesterday.
eng1-w4-q3.explanation: 'yesterday' is a specific, finished past time, so simple past 'met'. The most common trap is 'have met', but the present perfect is not used with a specific past time.

eng1-w4-q4.question: She ___ in Chennai since 2019.
eng1-w4-q4.explanation: 'since 2019' shows that the action began in the past and is still continuing, so present perfect 'has lived'. 'lives' or 'is living' is not used with since.

eng1-w4-q5.question: By the time we reached the station, the train ___.
eng1-w4-q5.explanation: There are two past actions: the train leaving happened first, and our reaching happened later. The earlier action takes the past perfect 'had left'. This pattern is very common in sentences with 'By the time'.

eng1-w4-q6.question: Which sentence is correct in standard English?
options: I have finished the work yesterday.
I am understanding your point now.
She has been owning this car for years.
He has lived here since he was a child.
eng1-w4-q6.explanation: 'has lived ... since' is a correct use of the present perfect. In option A the present perfect with 'yesterday' is wrong. In options B and C stative verbs (understand, own) are used in the continuous, which is considered wrong in standard academic English.

eng1-w4-q7.question: 'She has been studying for three hours.' Which tense is this?
eng1-w4-q7.explanation: 'has been + studying (-ing)' is the structure of the present perfect continuous: an action that started in the past and is still going on. 'is studying' would be present continuous, 'has studied' present perfect, and 'had been studying' past perfect continuous.

eng1-w4-q8.question: I ___ the answer to this question.
eng1-w4-q8.explanation: 'know' is a stative verb (a state of mind), so it is not used in the continuous: 'I know'. 'am knowing' is the most common mistake; 'knowing' and 'am know' are grammatically incomplete.

eng1-w4-q9.question: We booked our train tickets last week. We ___ visit Jaipur next month.
eng1-w4-q9.explanation: The tickets are already booked, so the plan was made earlier, and 'next month' is in the future, so 'are going to'. visited, have visited and had visited are all past forms, which do not go with 'next month'.

eng1-w4-q10.question: A: 'The phone is ringing.' B: 'Don't worry, I ___ it.'
eng1-w4-q10.explanation: B decides at this very moment to pick up the phone, and 'will' is used for an instant decision: 'I will answer it'. 'answered' and 'had answered' are past, but the action is still to happen, and 'I answer it' is the simple present of habits, which does not fit here.

eng1-w4-q11.question: When I reached home, my brother ___ dinner.
eng1-w4-q11.explanation: There are two past actions: my brother's dinner came first, my reaching home came later. The earlier past action takes the past perfect 'had already eaten'. 'has already eaten' is present perfect, which does not fit a past story ('reached'), and the other two options are present tense.

eng1-w4-q12.question: Which sentence uses the present perfect correctly?
options: She has just submitted her assignment.
They have gone to Shimla last summer.
Have you seen the match yesterday?
eng1-w4-q12.explanation: 'has just submitted' has no specific past time, and 'just' shows a link to the present, so it is correct. The other three have a specific past time (in 2022, last summer, yesterday), which needs the simple past: visited, went, did you see.

eng1-w4-q13.question: Choose the pair that fills both blanks: 'Ravi ___ in this company since 2021. Before that, he ___ in a bank for two years.'
eng1-w4-q13.explanation: First blank: 'since 2021' shows that this job is still going on, so the present perfect 'has worked'. Second blank: the bank job is over ('Before that'), so the simple past 'worked'. 'works ... since' is wrong, and 'has worked' does not fit a bank job that has ended.

eng1-w4-q14.question: Which sentence is correct in standard English?
options: I am having lunch right now.
We are owning a small shop.
eng1-w4-q14.explanation: 'have lunch' means to eat lunch, which is an action, so 'am having lunch' is perfectly correct. But 'having a car' (possession), 'knowing' and 'owning' are states, and stative verbs are not used in the continuous. Trap: thinking 'have' is always stative; check its meaning first.

eng1-w4-q15.question: Which time expression correctly completes 'I have read this novel ___'?
eng1-w4-q15.explanation: 'twice' tells us how many times, not a specific past time, so it fits the present perfect. 'last week', 'in 2023' and 'two days ago' are specific, finished past times; they need the simple past: 'I read this novel last week'.

eng1-w5-q1.question: Each of the students ___ a laptop.
eng1-w5-q1.explanation: The subject is 'Each', which is always singular, so 'has'. Trap: 'students' is plural, but it sits inside the 'of' phrase; it is not the real subject.

eng1-w5-q2.question: The news ___ good today.
eng1-w5-q2.explanation: 'news' ends in s, but it is an uncountable, singular noun, so 'is'. Don't assume it is plural just from the spelling.

eng1-w5-q3.question: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ ready for the test.
eng1-w5-q3.explanation: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here the nearer one is 'the students' (plural), so 'were'. 'was' would be correct if the order were reversed: 'Neither the students nor the teacher was ready.'

eng1-w5-q4.question: The captain, along with his players, ___ arrived at the ground.
eng1-w5-q4.explanation: 'along with his players' is extra information; the main subject 'The captain' is singular, so 'has'. Trap: because 'players' is close by, people pick 'have'.

eng1-w5-q5.question: A number of students ___ absent today.
eng1-w5-q5.explanation: 'A number of' means 'many', so the plural verb 'are'. 'The number of students is...' would take a singular verb, because there we are talking about a single count (number).

eng1-w5-q6.question: One of my friends ___ in Canada.
eng1-w5-q6.explanation: The real subject is 'One', not 'friends', so the singular verb 'lives'. Remember the pattern 'One of + plural noun': plural noun, singular verb.

eng1-w5-q7.question: Everyone in the class ___ excited about the trip.
eng1-w5-q7.explanation: 'Everyone' always takes a singular verb, so 'is'. Trap: 'everyone' includes many people and 'class' is a group too, so students pick the plural 'are'.

eng1-w5-q8.question: The advice my seniors gave me ___ really helpful.
eng1-w5-q8.explanation: 'advice' is an uncountable, singular noun, so it takes the singular verb 'was'. Trap: 'seniors' is plural, but it is not the subject; the real subject is 'The advice'.

eng1-w5-q9.question: My sister ___ to the gym every morning.
eng1-w5-q9.explanation: 'My sister' is a singular subject and this is a daily habit, so the simple present verb with -es: 'goes'. 'go' is for plural subjects (They go), and 'going' cannot be the verb on its own.

eng1-w5-q10.question: Either my parents or my brother ___ going to pick me up.
eng1-w5-q10.explanation: With either...or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here the nearer one is 'my brother' (singular), so 'is'. Trap: choosing 'are' because 'parents' is plural; 'are' would be right only with the order reversed: 'Either my brother or my parents are...'.

eng1-w5-q11.question: The number of applicants this year ___ higher than last year.
eng1-w5-q11.explanation: 'The number of' talks about a count, and a count is one thing, so it takes the singular verb 'is'. Trap: 'applicants' is plural, but a plural verb comes only with 'A number of' (many).

eng1-w5-q12.question: The box of chocolates that my aunts sent ___ on the table.
eng1-w5-q12.explanation: The real subject is 'The box'; 'of chocolates' and 'that my aunts sent' are only extra information. A box is singular, so 'is'. Traps: using 'are' or 'were' because of the plural nouns 'chocolates' and 'aunts' near the verb.

eng1-w5-q13.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: The teacher, as well as the students, were late.
Each of the players have a new kit.
A number of trees was cut down last week.
One of the shops near our college sells fresh bread.
eng1-w5-q13.explanation: In 'One of the shops' the subject is 'One', so the singular 'sells' is correct. In option A the main subject 'The teacher' is singular (the part after 'as well as' is extra), so it needs 'was'. In option B 'Each' is singular, so 'has'. In option C 'A number of trees' is plural, so 'were'.

eng1-w5-q14.question: Choose the pair that fills both blanks: 'The list of names ___ on the notice board, and a number of names ___ missing.'
eng1-w5-q14.explanation: First blank: the subject 'The list' is singular ('of names' is an extra phrase), so 'is'. Second blank: 'a number of names' means many names, so the plural 'are'. 'names' is near both blanks, but only the second takes a plural verb, because there it follows 'a number of'.

eng1-w5-q15.question: How many of these sentences are correct?
eng1-w5-q15.explanation: (1) is correct: Each = singular, has. (4) is correct: the main subject 'The principal' is singular, and the 'together with' part is extra. (2) is wrong: news is singular, so 'was'. (3) is wrong: with neither...nor the nearer subject 'his friends' is plural, so 'were'. So 2 sentences are correct.

eng1-w6-q1.question: She is ___ honest person.
eng1-w6-q1.explanation: In 'honest' the h is silent; the word begins with the vowel sound 'o', so 'an'. Using 'a' just because you see the letter h is the most common mistake.

eng1-w6-q2.question: There isn't ___ milk left in the fridge.
eng1-w6-q2.explanation: 'milk' is an uncountable noun and the sentence is negative, so 'much'. many, few and a few are used only with countable plural nouns (books, students).

eng1-w6-q3.question: Which phrase is correct?
eng1-w6-q3.explanation: The first sound of 'European' is 'yoo' (a consonant sound), so 'a European'. 'an university' (yoo sound), 'a hour' (h silent, vowel sound) and 'an one-day' (w sound) are all wrong.

eng1-w6-q4.question: ___ Ganga is a holy river for many Indians.
eng1-w6-q4.explanation: Names of rivers take 'the': the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Nile. Cities and countries (such as Delhi, India) take no article, and that is the source of confusion.

eng1-w6-q5.question: I have ___ good friends here, so I don't feel lonely.
eng1-w6-q5.explanation: 'friends' is countable and the sentence has a positive meaning (I don't feel lonely), so 'a few'. 'few' means 'very few, almost none', which doesn't match 'I don't feel lonely'. little/a little are for uncountable nouns.

eng1-w6-q6.question: Which sentence uses articles correctly?
options: The honesty is the best policy.
She plays the piano every evening.
He is best player in the team.
I had a breakfast at eight.
eng1-w6-q6.explanation: Musical instruments take 'the': 'plays the piano'. In option A the abstract noun 'honesty' is used in a general sense, so it takes no 'the'. In option C 'the' is missing before the superlative 'best'. In option D the simple meal 'breakfast' does not take 'a'.

eng1-w6-q7.question: ___ shoes are too tight for me.
eng1-w6-q7.explanation: 'shoes' is plural, and plural nouns take 'these' (or 'those'). 'This' and 'That' are for singular nouns, and 'A' never goes with a plural noun.

eng1-w6-q8.question: How ___ students attended the workshop?
eng1-w6-q8.explanation: 'students' is a countable plural noun, so 'many'. 'much', 'little' and 'a little' go with uncountable nouns (water, time).

eng1-w6-q9.question: Ananya is ___ tallest girl in our class.
eng1-w6-q9.explanation: Superlatives (tallest, best) take 'the', because there is only one tallest girl. 'a tallest' and 'Ananya is tallest girl' without an article are both wrong.

eng1-w6-q10.question: I bought ___ umbrella yesterday. ___ umbrella is already broken.
eng1-w6-q10.explanation: First blank: 'umbrella' begins with the vowel sound 'uh', so 'an umbrella'. Second blank: the same umbrella is mentioned again, so it is now specific: 'The'. 'a umbrella' breaks the sound rule, and using 'An' the second time forgets that the thing has already been mentioned.

eng1-w6-q11.question: There is ___ hope of rain today; the sky is completely clear.
eng1-w6-q11.explanation: The sky is completely clear, so there is almost no hope of rain (a negative meaning), and 'hope' is uncountable, so 'little'. 'a little' would be positive (there is some hope), and 'few' / 'a few' are for countable plural nouns.

eng1-w6-q12.question: Which sentence uses articles correctly?
options: He took a one-day trip to the Taj Mahal.
I will be there in a hour.
eng1-w6-q12.explanation: The first sound of 'one' is 'w' (a consonant sound), so 'a one-day trip' is correct. 'an university' is wrong (the sound is 'yoo'), 'a hour' is wrong (h is silent, so a vowel sound), and a city name like 'Delhi' takes no 'the'.

eng1-w6-q13.question: Fill in the blanks: 'My cousin is ___ MBA student. He plays ___ flute and loves ___ cricket.'
eng1-w6-q13.explanation: The first sound of 'MBA' is 'em' (a vowel sound), so 'an MBA'. A musical instrument takes 'the': 'plays the flute'. A sport takes no article: 'loves cricket'. Traps: using 'a' because M is a consonant letter, and swapping the rules for instruments and sports.

eng1-w6-q14.question: How many article mistakes are there in this sentence? 'I had a lunch with an European friend near the Yamuna.'
eng1-w6-q14.explanation: There are two mistakes: (1) a simple meal like 'lunch' takes no article, so 'had lunch'; (2) the first sound of 'European' is 'yoo' (a consonant sound), so 'a European'. 'the Yamuna' is correct, because river names take 'the'. Trap: counting 'the Yamuna' as a mistake too and saying 3.

eng1-w6-q15.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: There aren't much chairs in the hall.
How many water do you drink daily?
She has a few patience with noisy kids.
I have little money, so I can't buy it now.
eng1-w6-q15.explanation: 'money' is uncountable, and 'so I can't buy it' shows a negative meaning, so 'little money' is correct. 'chairs' is countable, so 'many chairs'; 'water' is uncountable, so 'How much water'; and 'patience' is uncountable, so 'a little patience' (not a few).

eng1-w7-q1.question: The class starts ___ 9 a.m.
eng1-w7-q1.explanation: An exact clock time takes 'at': at 9 a.m. 'on' is for days/dates and 'in' is for months/years.

eng1-w7-q2.question: My birthday is ___ 15 August.
eng1-w7-q2.explanation: A specific date takes 'on': on 15 August. 'in August' would be correct if it were only the month, but with a date only 'on' is used.

eng1-w7-q3.question: I have been waiting ___ two hours.
eng1-w7-q3.explanation: 'two hours' is a duration (how long), so 'for'. 'since' is used only with a starting point, as in 'since 4 p.m.'.

eng1-w7-q4.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: We discussed regarding about the plan.
eng1-w7-q4.explanation: 'discuss' is followed directly by its object, with no preposition: 'discussed the plan'. 'discussed about' is a common mistake that comes from the Hindi 'ke baare mein'. (With the noun, 'a discussion about' is correct.)

eng1-w7-q5.question: The teacher divided the sweets ___ all the students in the class.
eng1-w7-q5.explanation: The whole class is one group, so 'among'. 'between' is used for two people (or people clearly named one by one).

eng1-w7-q6.question: Which sentence uses the preposition correctly?
options: They reached at the station late.
eng1-w7-q6.explanation: 'depend on' is the correct fixed combination. The other three are wrong: 'good at mathematics', 'interested in music', and 'reached the station' (reach does not take 'at').

eng1-w7-q7.question: We usually visit the hills ___ May.
eng1-w7-q7.explanation: Months take 'in': in May, in July. 'on' is for days and dates (on 5 May), and 'at' is for an exact time (at 5 p.m.).

eng1-w7-q8.question: She is waiting for you ___ the bus stop.
eng1-w7-q8.explanation: A bus stop is a point (a spot), so 'at'. 'on' is for a surface (on the table), 'into' for movement inside something, and 'among' for being within a group.

eng1-w7-q9.question: This song was composed ___ my music teacher.
eng1-w7-q9.explanation: In a passive sentence the doer (agent) takes 'by': composed by my music teacher. 'with' is for a tool (write with a pen), not for the agent.

eng1-w7-q10.question: I have known Neha ___ Class 6, so we have been friends ___ many years.
eng1-w7-q10.explanation: 'Class 6' is a starting point, so 'since'. 'many years' is a duration, so 'for'. Trap: using the same preposition in both blanks; after each blank, check whether it is a point or a duration.

eng1-w7-q11.question: My little brother is afraid ___ dogs.
eng1-w7-q11.explanation: The fixed combination is 'afraid of'. 'afraid from' is a direct translation of the Hindi 'se darna', and it is wrong in English.

eng1-w7-q12.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: She entered into the room in the morning.
She is married with a doctor.
He is good at chess and interested in music.
We reached at Delhi late at night.
eng1-w7-q12.explanation: 'good at' and 'interested in' are both correct fixed combinations. In 'entered into the room' the 'into' should go (enter takes a direct object), 'married with' should be 'married to', and 'reached at Delhi' should have no 'at'.

eng1-w7-q13.question: How many preposition mistakes are there in this sentence? 'I am angry on Ravi because he did not attend to the meeting on Friday.'
eng1-w7-q13.explanation: There are two mistakes: (1) being angry at a person is 'angry with Ravi', not 'angry on'; (2) 'attend' takes no preposition: 'attend the meeting'. 'on Friday' is correct, because days take 'on'. Trap: counting 'on Friday' as a mistake too (3).

eng1-w7-q14.question: Which sentence has an extra preposition that should be removed?
options: He is afraid of the dark.
She asked to me a question.
eng1-w7-q14.explanation: 'ask' takes a direct object: 'She asked me a question'. So the 'to' is extra. In the other three the preposition is needed: afraid of, depends on, interested in.

eng1-w7-q15.question: Which sentence uses 'since' or 'for' correctly?
options: I have been here since two hours.
We have not met since last Diwali.
He has lived in Goa since five years.
eng1-w7-q15.explanation: 'last Diwali' is a point in time, so 'since last Diwali' is correct. 'two hours' and 'five years' are durations, so they need 'for', and '2015' is a starting point, so 'since 2015'.

eng1-w8-q1.question: What type of sentence is 'Please close the door.'?
eng1-w8-q1.explanation: This is a request/instruction with a hidden subject 'you', so it is imperative. Don't take it as declarative just because of the full stop; a declarative sentence only gives information.

eng1-w8-q2.question: What type of sentence is 'What a beautiful view this is!'?
eng1-w8-q2.explanation: It shows a strong feeling (surprise/admiration) and follows the 'What a ...!' pattern, so it is exclamatory. Even though it starts with 'What', it is not a question, because the word order is that of a statement and it ends with '!'.

eng1-w8-q3.question: 'I wanted to go out, but it was raining.' This sentence is:
eng1-w8-q3.explanation: Two independent clauses ('I wanted to go out' and 'it was raining') are joined by the coordinating conjunction 'but', so it is compound. It would be complex if one clause were dependent (e.g. starting with because/although).

eng1-w8-q4.question: 'Although she was tired, she finished the assignment.' This sentence is:
eng1-w8-q4.explanation: 'Although she was tired' is a dependent clause (not complete on its own), and 'she finished the assignment' is an independent clause. Dependent + independent = complex sentence.

eng1-w8-q5.question: Which is a correctly formed indirect question?
options: Can you tell me where is the bank?
Can you tell me where does the bank is?
Can you tell me the bank where is?
Can you tell me where the bank is?
eng1-w8-q5.explanation: The part after 'Can you tell me' comes in statement order: subject (the bank) + verb (is). 'where is the bank' is direct-question order, which is wrong here.

eng1-w8-q6.question: Which option is correctly punctuated?
options: The exam was easy, I finished early.
The exam was easy I finished early.
The exam was easy; I finished early.
eng1-w8-q6.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses. Option A is a comma splice, option B is a run-on (no punctuation), and option D is a fragment (only a dependent clause).

eng1-w8-q7.question: What type of sentence is 'Where does your brother study?'?
eng1-w8-q7.explanation: This sentence asks a question: the auxiliary 'does' comes before the subject 'your brother' and it ends with '?', so it is interrogative. A declarative sentence only gives information, and an imperative is an order or request.

eng1-w8-q8.question: Which of these is a simple sentence?
options: I was tired, so I slept early.
When I reached, the class had begun.
My cousin studies data science in Chennai.
eng1-w8-q8.explanation: Option C has only one independent clause (one subject 'My cousin' + one verb 'studies'), so it is a simple sentence. Option A is compound (two clauses joined by 'so'), option B is complex (a dependent 'When' clause), and option D is a fragment.

eng1-w8-q9.question: Which of these is a coordinating conjunction (one of FANBOYS)?
eng1-w8-q9.explanation: FANBOYS = for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so; 'yet' is one of them. because, although and when begin a dependent clause, as in complex sentences.

eng1-w8-q10.question: 'If you finish early, you can leave.' This sentence is:
eng1-w8-q10.explanation: 'If you finish early' is a dependent clause (not complete on its own), and 'you can leave' is an independent clause. Dependent + independent = complex. A compound sentence needs two independent clauses joined by FANBOYS.

eng1-w8-q11.question: Which is the correct question form of 'She studies physics'?
eng1-w8-q11.explanation: In a simple present question the auxiliary 'does' comes before the subject, and the main verb is in its base form: 'Does she study'. 'Does she studies' marks the -s twice, 'Do she' uses 'do' with a singular subject, and 'Is she study' uses the wrong auxiliary.

eng1-w8-q12.question: Which option is a sentence fragment?
options: It rained, and we stayed in.
eng1-w8-q12.explanation: 'Although the bus was late.' is a dependent clause; it needs a main clause (such as '..., we reached on time'), so it is a fragment. Trap: 'Sit down.' is short but it is a complete imperative sentence with the hidden subject 'you'. 'She smiled.' is a simple sentence and option D is compound.

eng1-w8-q13.question: How many independent clauses are there in 'I called her, but she did not answer because her phone was off'?
eng1-w8-q13.explanation: 'I called her' and 'she did not answer' are both independent clauses joined by 'but': a total of 2. 'because her phone was off' is a dependent clause, because it cannot stand alone as a complete sentence. Trap: counting every clause and saying 3.

eng1-w8-q14.question: Which sentence is correct?
options: Could you tell me how much this costs?
Please tell me what is your name.
I wonder why is he late.
Do you know where does she live?
eng1-w8-q14.explanation: An indirect question uses statement order (subject + verb): 'how much this costs'. The other three wrongly keep direct-question order; the correct forms are 'what your name is', 'why he is late' and 'where she lives'.

eng1-w8-q15.question: Which is the correct exclamatory form of 'She is a very talented singer.'?
options: How a talented singer she is!
Is she a very talented singer!
What a talented singer she is!
eng1-w8-q15.explanation: With a singular countable noun the pattern is 'What a + adjective + noun + subject + verb!': 'What a talented singer she is!'. Option A is missing 'a', option B wrongly uses 'How a' ('How' is followed directly by an adjective, as in 'How talented she is!'), and option C is question order with a '!' added.

eng1-w9-q1.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'rapid'.
eng1-w9-q1.explanation: 'rapid' means very fast, so the synonym is 'quick'. 'slow' is its antonym, and heavy/calm have no direct relation to speed.

eng1-w9-q2.question: Choose the correct opposite of 'possible'.
eng1-w9-q2.explanation: With words starting with 'p', the prefix 'in-' changes to 'im-': impossible, impatient, impolite. The other three are not English words.

eng1-w9-q3.question: Please don't ___ a mistake while filling the form.
eng1-w9-q3.explanation: The natural collocation is 'make a mistake'. 'do a mistake' is heard in Indian English but is considered wrong in standard English. 'do' goes with homework, work, exercise.

eng1-w9-q4.question: The meeting has been ___ till Friday because the manager is unwell.
eng1-w9-q4.explanation: 'put off' = to postpone, push to a later time, which matches the context here. 'put on' = to wear (put on a jacket), 'put out' = to put out a fire or switch off a light.

eng1-w9-q5.question: We had very ___ rain last night, and the roads were flooded.
eng1-w9-q5.explanation: The natural collocation with rain is 'heavy rain'. 'strong rain' is a direct translation of the Hindi 'tez baarish'; 'strong' goes with wind or coffee, not with rain.

eng1-w9-q6.question: Lack of sleep can badly ___ your memory.
eng1-w9-q6.explanation: After 'can' we need a base verb meaning 'to have an influence on', so 'affect'. 'effect' is mostly a noun (a bad effect); 'effects' is a plural noun, and 'affection' means love.

eng1-w9-q7.question: Choose the correct opposite of 'legal'.
eng1-w9-q7.explanation: For words beginning with 'l', the prefix 'in-' changes to 'il-': illegal, illogical. unlegal, inlegal and dislegal are not English words.

eng1-w9-q8.question: Choose the word closest in meaning to 'enormous'.
eng1-w9-q8.explanation: 'enormous' means very big, so the closest synonym is 'huge'. 'tiny' is its opposite (antonym), and quiet and early have nothing to do with size.

eng1-w9-q9.question: Who will ___ your dog while you are away?
eng1-w9-q9.explanation: 'look after' = take care of, which fits here. 'look up' = search for in a dictionary, 'look into' = investigate something, and 'look down on' = think someone is inferior.

eng1-w9-q10.question: Which word means 'to judge something wrongly'?
eng1-w9-q10.explanation: The prefix 'mis-' means 'wrong' (as in misunderstand), so 'misjudge' = judge wrongly. Trap: 'pre-' means 'before', so 'prejudge' = judge beforehand, not wrongly.

eng1-w9-q11.question: My teacher ___ me to revise every day.
eng1-w9-q11.explanation: A verb is needed here (gave advice), and the verb is 'advise', whose past form is 'advised'. 'advice' is a noun, 'advices' is not used (advice is uncountable), and 'adviced' is not a word at all.

eng1-w9-q12.question: Read: 'Ravi is usually very talkative, but today he was taciturn and hardly said a word.' Here, 'taciturn' most nearly means:
eng1-w9-q12.explanation: Context clues: 'but' shows a contrast, so taciturn must be the opposite of 'talkative', and 'hardly said a word' tells us he spoke very little. So 'silent and reserved'. 'very talkative' ignores the contrast word, and the text gives no clue for angry or tired.

eng1-w9-q13.question: Which sentence uses 'lose' and 'loose' correctly?
options: If you lose focus, you may loose the match.
My shirt feels loose, and I don't want to lose more weight.
eng1-w9-q13.explanation: 'loose' = not tight (adjective) and 'lose' = fail to keep (verb). In option D the shirt is not tight (loose) and the weight is something to lose (lose), so both are right. Options A and B swap the words, and in option C the first 'lose' is right but 'loose the match' is wrong.

eng1-w9-q14.question: Which option has ALL natural collocations?
options: do homework, heavy rain, pay attention
make homework, heavy rain, pay attention
do homework, strong rain, pay attention
do homework, heavy rain, do attention
eng1-w9-q14.explanation: The natural pairs are 'do homework', 'heavy rain' and 'pay attention'; option A has all three. Every other option has one mistake: 'make homework', 'strong rain' (a translation of the Hindi 'tez baarish') and 'do attention'.

eng1-w9-q15.question: Choose the pair that fills both blanks: 'We have ___ milk, so I'll go to the shop. Also, the match has been ___ till Sunday because of the rain.'
eng1-w9-q15.explanation: First blank: the milk is finished, so 'run out of'. Second blank: the match was postponed, so 'put off'. 'given up milk' means stopped drinking milk, which is no reason to go to the shop, and 'turned down' means refused, not postponed.

eng1-w10-q1.question: Notice: 'The library will stay open till 10 p.m. from Monday to Friday, and till 6 p.m. on Saturday. It remains closed on Sunday.' Till what time is the library open on Saturday?
eng1-w10-q1.explanation: Scan the text: next to the keyword 'Saturday' it says '6 p.m.'. 10 p.m. is for weekdays and 'closed' is for Sunday; those are the traps.

eng1-w10-q2.question: Read: 'Drinking enough water helps the body control its temperature. It also keeps joints moving smoothly and helps the kidneys remove waste.' What is the main idea?
options: Kidneys remove waste from the body.
Water helps the body in several ways.
eng1-w10-q2.explanation: The whole text describes the different benefits of water, so the main idea is 'Water helps the body in several ways'. Option A is only one supporting detail; options C and D are not in the text at all.

eng1-w10-q3.question: Read: 'Arjun practised every day for a month. ___, he still felt nervous before the debate.' Which word fits best?
eng1-w10-q3.explanation: Still feeling nervous after practising every day is a contrast (the opposite of what is expected), so 'However'. 'Therefore' would show a result, such as becoming confident because of the practice.

eng1-w10-q4.question: Read: 'The hall was so cramped that people had to stand shoulder to shoulder, and some could not even get in.' Here, 'cramped' most nearly means:
eng1-w10-q4.explanation: Context clue: people stood shoulder to shoulder and some could not even get in, which means there was little space and a big crowd. So 'too small and crowded'.

eng1-w10-q5.question: Read: 'Meera runs a tea stall near a college. She opens at 6 a.m. and offers a cheaper cup to students who bring their own steel tumbler.' Statement: 'Meera's stall is the only tea stall near the college.' This statement is:
eng1-w10-q5.explanation: The text gives no information about other tea stalls, neither yes nor no. So 'Not Given'. It would be 'False' if the text said there were other stalls there too.

eng1-w10-q6.question: Read: 'When Meera started the offer, only a few students brought tumblers. By the end of the semester, almost half her customers were carrying them, and the road outside looked much cleaner.' Which inference is best supported by the text?
options: Most students refused the offer for the whole year.
Students' habits changed gradually over the semester.
Meera stopped using paper cups completely.
The college gave Meera an award for her idea.
eng1-w10-q6.explanation: 'a few' at the start and 'almost half' at the end show that the change happened gradually, so option B is best supported. Option A contradicts the text, option C is not stated (only half the customers brought tumblers), and option D is not mentioned at all.

eng1-w10-q7.question: You want to find only the date of the exam in a long notice. Which reading skill should you use?
eng1-w10-q7.explanation: To find a specific piece of information (a date) you scan: instead of reading the whole notice slowly, look only for the keyword or number. Skimming is for the overall idea (gist), and inference is for working out what the text implies.

eng1-w10-q8.question: In 'The bus was late; therefore, we missed the first lecture', what does 'therefore' show?
eng1-w10-q8.explanation: Missing the lecture is the result of the bus being late, and 'therefore' shows a result. A contrast uses however/but, an example uses 'for example', and an addition uses 'moreover'.

eng1-w10-q9.question: Notice: 'Registration for the coding club closes on 14 March. The fee is ₹200 for first-year students and ₹300 for all others. Contact Kavya in Room 12.' How much will a second-year student pay?
eng1-w10-q9.explanation: Scan the notice: a second-year student is not a first-year, so they fall under 'all others', whose fee is ₹300. ₹200 is only for first-years, ₹500 is the two fees added together, which the text never mentions, and 12 is the room number.

eng1-w10-q10.question: Text: 'The Excel workshop will be held online on Saturday. Participants must register by Thursday.' Statement: 'The workshop will take place in the college auditorium.' This statement is:
eng1-w10-q10.explanation: The text clearly says the workshop will be online, which contradicts the auditorium claim, so it is False. Trap: the word 'auditorium' is not in the text, so students pick 'Not Given'; but when the text says the opposite, the answer is False.

eng1-w10-q11.question: Read: 'Many students study late into the night. However, studies show that a regular sleep schedule improves memory. Students who sleep at fixed times often score better than those who stay up late.' What is the main idea?
options: Many students study late into the night.
Research is hard for students to follow.
Students should never study at night.
A regular sleep schedule helps students perform better.
eng1-w10-q11.explanation: The paragraph makes its real point after 'However': sleeping at fixed times improves memory and marks. Option A is only the opening detail that the text argues against, option C is a stronger claim than the text makes ('never'), and option B is not mentioned at all.

eng1-w10-q12.question: Text: 'The city library opened a new reading room in June. It has 40 seats and is open only to members. Membership costs ₹500 a year, but students pay half.' Which statement is TRUE according to the text?
options: Anyone can use the new reading room.
A student pays ₹250 a year for membership.
It is the largest reading room in the city.
The reading room opened in July.
eng1-w10-q12.explanation: Membership is ₹500 and students pay half: 500 ÷ 2 = ₹250, so option B is True. Option A is False (the room is only for members), option D is False (it opened in June), and option C is Not Given, because the text does not compare it with any other reading room.

eng1-w10-q13.question: Read: 'When the power went off, Aman lit a candle and kept solving his physics problems. His roommate, however, put away his books and went to sleep.' Which inference is best supported by the text?
options: Aman was more determined to keep studying than his roommate.
Aman's roommate was ill that night.
The power cut lasted the whole night.
eng1-w10-q13.explanation: Even after the power went off, Aman lit a candle and kept studying, while his roommate put his books away; 'however' marks exactly this contrast. So option A is best supported. The text says nothing about the roommate being ill, how long the power cut lasted, or whether Aman's answers were right; those are pure imagination.

eng1-w10-q14.question: Arrange the sentences P, Q, R and S in the most logical order.
eng1-w10-q14.explanation: Q, with 'First', comes at the start and P, with 'Finally', at the end. S says 'Once your details are saved', so the details (R) must be filled in first, which puts S after R. Order: Q R S P. Trap: QSRP, which ignores the clue 'Once your details are saved' in S.

eng1-w10-q15.question: Announcement: 'Attention, please. The 5:30 p.m. train to Mysuru will now leave from platform 4 instead of platform 2. It is running 15 minutes late.' When and from where will the train now leave?
eng1-w10-q15.explanation: The train is 15 minutes late, so 5:30 + 15 minutes = 5:45 p.m. The platform has changed to 4 ('instead of platform 2'). Traps: remembering the old platform 2, or subtracting the 15 minutes instead of adding them (5:15).

eng1-w11-q1.question: You meet someone for the first time at a seminar. What is the most appropriate thing to say?
eng1-w11-q1.explanation: On a first meeting we say 'Nice to meet you'. 'see you again' and 'Long time no see' are used when you already know the person, and 'What's up, buddy?' is far too informal for a seminar.

eng1-w11-q2.question: Which is the most polite way to ask a classmate for their notes?
options: Could you please lend me your notes?
eng1-w11-q2.explanation: 'Could you please...?' is the standard pattern for a polite request. The other options sound like orders and can come across as rude, even if the grammar is correct.

eng1-w11-q3.question: Which topic is the safest for small talk with a new classmate?
options: How they found today's live session
eng1-w11-q3.explanation: A shared experience such as the course or today's class is a safe and easy topic. Income, religion and weight are personal or sensitive topics that should be avoided in a first conversation.

eng1-w11-q4.question: A classmate says, 'I'm from Kochi.' Which reply best keeps the conversation going?
options: Oh, nice! What's it like living there?
eng1-w11-q4.explanation: An open follow-up question gives the other person a chance to say more, so the conversation keeps going. 'Okay' and 'Hmm' end the conversation, and the last option changes the topic rudely.

eng1-w11-q5.question: Which sentence is correct in standard English for a self-introduction?
options: I am having two years of work experience.
I have two years of work experience.
I am knowing Python and SQL.
eng1-w11-q5.explanation: 'have' here shows possession (a state), so the simple present 'I have' is correct. 'am having' and 'am knowing' are wrong continuous uses of stative verbs, and 'Myself Rahul' is not a standard introduction.

eng1-w11-q6.question: In a formal online interview, the interviewer says, 'Tell me about yourself.' Which opening is most appropriate?
options: Myself Anjali, I am from Lucknow only.
Good morning. I'm Anjali Verma, a first-year BS Data Science student from Lucknow.
Hi, what exactly do you want to know?
Everything is already written in my resume.
eng1-w11-q6.explanation: Option B has a greeting, the full name and relevant background in a polite, formal tone. In option A 'Myself' and 'only' are Indianisms, option C sounds casual and defensive, and option D avoids the question.

eng1-w11-q7.question: You meet a school friend after a year. What is the most natural thing to say?
eng1-w11-q7.explanation: When you meet someone you already know, you say 'Nice to see you again'. 'Nice to meet you' is only for a first meeting, 'Good night' is said when leaving (not as a greeting), and 'Myself Rohan' is not standard English.

eng1-w11-q8.question: You enter a formal interview room at 10 a.m. Which greeting is most appropriate?
eng1-w11-q8.explanation: The setting is formal and it is morning, so 'Good morning.' 'Hey, what's up?' and 'Yo, guys!' are far too informal, and 'Good night' is a phrase for leaving, not a greeting.

eng1-w11-q9.question: A new classmate asks, 'How are you?' Which reply is the most appropriate?
options: I'm fine, thanks. How about you?
eng1-w11-q9.explanation: 'I'm fine, thanks. How about you?' is polite and keeps the conversation going by returning the question. 'Why do you ask?' sounds rude, salary is a sensitive topic, and 'Fine. Bye.' ends the conversation at once.

eng1-w11-q10.question: Which sentence is best for a formal self-introduction?
options: I passed out from Delhi University in 2023.
I am passed out from Delhi University.
I have passed out from Delhi University in 2023.
I graduated from Delhi University in 2023.
eng1-w11-q10.explanation: In standard English, finishing a degree is 'graduated from'. The standard meaning of 'pass out' is to faint, so the other three options are Indianisms (and option C also wrongly uses the present perfect with a specific past time like '2023').

eng1-w11-q11.question: Which question should you AVOID asking someone you have just met?
options: How was your trip to Ooty?
eng1-w11-q11.explanation: Salary (income) is a personal, sensitive topic that should be avoided when you first meet someone. Course, hobbies (cricket) and travel are safe small-talk topics.

eng1-w11-q12.question: Arrange these lines into the best self-introduction.
eng1-w11-q12.explanation: The structure of a self-introduction is: greeting (Q), name and background (S), what you are doing now (P), then a polite closing (R). So Q S P R. 'SQPR' gives the name before the greeting, 'QPSR' gives the course before the name, and 'QSRP' adds new information after the closing.

eng1-w11-q13.question: How many of these lines from a self-introduction need to be corrected?
eng1-w11-q13.explanation: (1) is wrong: 'I'm Sana' instead of 'Myself Sana'. (3) is wrong: 'know' is a stative verb, so 'I know Excel well'. (2) and (4) are perfectly correct. So 2 lines need correcting. Trap: confusing 'I graduated from college' with 'passed out' and counting it as wrong.

eng1-w11-q14.question: A new classmate says, 'I spent the weekend at a hackathon.' Which reply is an open follow-up question that best keeps the conversation going?
options: Oh, interesting! What did your team build?
eng1-w11-q14.explanation: 'What did your team build?' is an open question: it cannot be answered with just yes or no, so the other person will talk in detail. 'Did you go alone?' and 'Was it on Saturday?' are closed (yes/no) questions that stop at a one-word answer, and 'Okay.' ends the conversation.

eng1-w11-q15.question: A professor you met last month at a workshop says, 'Good to see you again, Rahul.' Which reply is most appropriate?
options: Good to see you too, Professor.
eng1-w11-q15.explanation: You have met the professor before and the setting is formal, so 'Good to see you too, Professor.' Trap: 'Nice to meet you' is only for a first meeting. 'Yo, what's up?' is far too casual for a professor, and 'Myself Rahul' is an Indianism.

eng1-w12-q1.question: Which is the best subject line for an email asking for more time to submit an assignment?
options: Request for extension of Week 4 assignment deadline
eng1-w12-q1.explanation: A good subject line is specific and tells the reader the purpose without opening the email. 'Hi', 'Urgent!!!' and 'please read this' are vague and look unprofessional.

eng1-w12-q2.question: Which is the most appropriate salutation for an email to a professor whose name you know?
eng1-w12-q2.explanation: In a formal email, 'Dear' + title + surname is standard: 'Dear Professor Iyer,'. The other three are far too casual and don't sound respectful to a professor.

eng1-w12-q3.question: Which sentence works best as the topic sentence of a paragraph on the benefits of online learning?
options: I logged in at 7 p.m. yesterday.
Some lecture videos are twenty minutes long.
Online learning gives students flexibility in where and when they study.
In conclusion, that is all I have to say.
eng1-w12-q3.explanation: A topic sentence states the main idea of the paragraph, and option C directly introduces a 'benefit' (flexibility). Options A and B are small details, and option D is like a conclusion, not an opening.

eng1-w12-q4.question: I wanted to avoid last-minute stress. ___, I started the assignment a week early.
eng1-w12-q4.explanation: The second sentence is the result of the first (I wanted to avoid stress, so I started early), so 'Therefore'. 'However' shows contrast, and 'Although' / 'Despite' are not used alone like this with a comma at the start of a sentence.

eng1-w12-q5.question: Which closing is most suitable for a formal email to a course instructor?
eng1-w12-q5.explanation: 'Regards' with the full name is a safe, professional closing. 'Love' is personal, 'Bye bye!' is conversational, and 'TTYL' is a chat abbreviation that doesn't work in a formal email.

eng1-w12-q6.question: A paragraph argues that students should sleep 7 to 8 hours before an exam. Which sentence does NOT belong in it?
options: Sleep helps the brain store what we studied during the day.
Many hostels serve breakfast at 7:30 a.m.
A tired mind makes more careless mistakes in calculations.
Students who rest well usually concentrate better in the exam hall.
eng1-w12-q6.explanation: The hostel breakfast time has nothing to do with sleep and exam performance, so it breaks the unity of the paragraph. The other three sentences directly support 'why sleep is important'.

eng1-w12-q7.question: Which linker shows ADDITION (adding one more point)?
eng1-w12-q7.explanation: 'Moreover' is used to add one more point (addition). 'However' shows contrast, 'Therefore' a result, and 'Although' also starts a contrasting dependent clause.

eng1-w12-q8.question: In a well-written paragraph, which sentence states the main idea?
eng1-w12-q8.explanation: The topic sentence states the paragraph's main idea; supporting and example sentences back that idea up. A subject line belongs to an email, not to a paragraph.

eng1-w12-q9.question: Which phrase is suitable for a formal email?
options: I would be grateful if you could
eng1-w12-q9.explanation: 'I would be grateful if you could...' is a polite, formal phrase. 'plz', 'asap' and 'u' are chat short forms, and ALL CAPS reads like shouting, so they don't belong in a formal email.

eng1-w12-q10.question: In a formal email, what should come right after the salutation (for example, 'Dear Professor Iyer,')?
options: An opening line that states the purpose
eng1-w12-q10.explanation: Right after the salutation, the opening line should state the purpose of the email, so the reader knows at once what it is about. The closing and full name come at the end, and the subject line comes before the salutation (at the top of the email).

eng1-w12-q11.question: Which is the best concluding sentence for a paragraph on why students should follow a regular study timetable?
options: Therefore, a fixed timetable helps students learn steadily and avoid stress.
My friend usually studies late at night after dinner.
First, make a list of all the subjects you need to study.
However, some subjects are much harder than the others.
eng1-w12-q11.explanation: A concluding sentence sums up the main idea, and option A wraps up the benefit of a timetable with 'Therefore'. Option B is an unrelated detail, option C sounds like the start of instructions, and option D opens a new contrast instead of concluding.

eng1-w12-q12.question: Choose the linkers for both blanks: 'Online classes save travel time. ___, they let students replay lectures. ___, some students find it hard to stay focused at home.'
eng1-w12-q12.explanation: First blank: replaying lectures is one more benefit of online classes, so addition: 'Moreover'. Second blank: finding it hard to focus at home is a problem, the opposite of the benefits, so contrast: 'However'. Option A swaps the two, and 'Therefore' is wrong because replaying lectures is not a result of saving travel time.

eng1-w12-q13.question: What is the main weakness of this email?
eng1-w12-q13.explanation: The salutation ('Dear Professor Menon,'), the purpose in the opening line, the polite request and the closing ('Regards' + full name) are all fine. Only the subject line 'Hi' is vague; it should be something like 'Request for extension of Week 9 assignment deadline'.

eng1-w12-q14.question: Which option correctly names the roles of sentence (1) and sentence (4)?
eng1-w12-q14.explanation: Sentence (1) states the main idea of the whole paragraph (the benefits of cycling), so it is the topic sentence. Sentences (2) and (3) give the benefits (supporting). Sentence (4) wraps up the idea with 'Clearly', so it is the concluding sentence. Trap: (4) is also general, but it does not introduce the idea at the start; it sums up at the end.

eng1-w12-q15.question: Arrange these parts of a formal email in the correct order.
eng1-w12-q15.explanation: The order of a formal email is: salutation (Q), the purpose in the opening line (R), a clear request (S), and finally the closing + name (P). So Q R S P. 'QSRP' puts the request before the purpose, 'RQSP' starts writing before the salutation, and 'QRPS' puts the request after the closing.
